t: When You Find Yourself Far Behind, Reset the Clock
q: When teams get blown away and find themselves in a lopsided game, the best coaches take a pause (halftime) and reset the score to 0-0.
People naturally feel hopeless and become demotivated whenever they are significantly behind in their commitments, goals, and desired outcomes.

Mentally resetting the score or clock allows performers to reframe the situation as a fresh start and to focus their attention on immediate effort and improvement instead of the daunting challenge of catching up.
Going from outcome-focused to process-oriented restores confidence and makes it easier to bounce back from any new obstacle or adversity.
People perform best when they focus on process over outcomes.

t: The Power of Retrieval: Helping Students Remember When It Counts
q: Retrieval practice is the act of bringing information to mind from memory, rather than re-reading or re-watching it. Several studies in cognitive science confirm that retrieving information strengthens memory far more than passive review. Each act of recall creates stronger, more accessible memory traces, slowing forgetting and making knowledge available when it counts, on the test, and beyond it.

This is why I not only teach to the test, but retrieve to it. My goal is to intentionally weave retrieval opportunities into daily instruction so students rehearse and strengthen what they’ll need to remember when it matters most.
The power of flashcards lies not in the cards themselves but in how they are used. When students quiz themselves, rather than simply reviewing, they benefit from the testing effect.

Brain dumps strip retrieval down to its most essential form. They create desirable difficulty by removing prompts and requiring students to self-generate recall. This both reveals the strength of their memory and surfaces the areas that need reinforcement.

The act of writing, rather than speaking, adds an extra layer of cognitive effort. It slows students down, requiring them to process their thinking more deliberately. The public nature of whiteboards raises the stakes slightly, making the retrieval more effortful and memorable.
Retrieval should not be occasional or incidental. It should be structured, cumulative, and aligned with the learning intention.

More importantly, it reframes what school is for: not rehearsing for a performance, but developing durable and accessible knowledge. Retrieval helps students see themselves as learners who can actively draw upon what they know, rather than hoping it will resurface when needed.

t: AI is Unwriting the Leadership Playbook
q: Even the leaders, the forward-thinkers, are asking the wrong question: "How do we add AI to what we're already doing?" The right question is: "What does AI reveal about what we should have been doing all along?
It's a structural change. And if you try to "implement AI" with the same habits that made sense in yesterday's system, you’re going to miss the opportunity to transform.

Too often, leaders jump straight to policies, firewalls, or training programs without truly understanding what problem they're solving. AI requires leaders to pause, suspend judgment, and invite deeper inquiry.

When someone raises concerns about AI, resist the urge to explain why they're wrong. Instead, try: "Help me understand how you're thinking about this." You might discover they're seeing something you've missed.
You can't just "bolt AI on" to your current processes (as AI likes to say). That's assimilation, and it leads to expensive failure.
This complexity creates paralysis. Nobody can remember all the rules, so they either do nothing or ignore them entirely.

But feedback is always late. By the time you've course-corrected, the damage is done. Transformation requires feedforward—clear, directive guidance that sets the floor for future action. Not "here's what you did wrong" but "here's what good looks like.

t: What's the Difference Between an A-Player and the B's & C's
q: Here's a simple scheme: A-players just need a goal. Once they know the desired outcome, they can figure out how to get there.
B-players need the goal and the strategy or approach to achieve it. They depend on leaders to help them think through the various choices or options and what game plan is best to ensure success.
C-players need more than the goal and the strategy. They need the tactics, too.

B-players need practice thinking of strategies and approaches to problems and goals. Dissecting existing strategies and creating new ones is how B-players gain the confidence and acumen to fly on their own.
Good leaders do more than simply recruit A-players to join their teams. They do the hard work it takes to elevate the talents, skills, and potential of everyone on the team, including the C-players.

C-players develop by identifying and prioritizing the tactical steps within a given strategy, building the connective tissue they currently lack.

t: Do we REALLY want Teachers to be more like Doctors?
q: In other words, teachers are like doctors–and doctors are like teachers. They’re just human beings, who are heavily biased towards stasis. And it’s hard to change people’s beliefs and attitudes, especially when they’ve been prescribing the same medication or teaching reading the same way for the last 20 plus years.

But according to Thomas Guskey, this theory of professional development rests on old and outdated research from the 1930s. There is little indication that this sort of knowledge-first professional development impacts teacher practice, especially among veteran teachers.

Guskey’s model argues that teacher beliefs and attitudes change only after they change their practice and see the impact on student learning. In Guskey’s telling, “the crucial point is that it is not the professional development per se, but the experience of successful implementation that changes teachers’ attitudes and beliefs. They believe it works because they have seen it work, and that experience shapes their attitudes and beliefs.” In other words? Doing and seeing enable believing.

Professional development should be more practical and less theoretical. It should be designed to get teachers implementing and experimenting with the desired practice or materials as quickly as possible. To achieve this, it also needs to include models (videos!) of other teachers teaching, opportunities for teacher rehearsal, prepared materials–whatever it takes to get teachers doing the work.

Even with all of the best supports in place, changing instructional practice is hard work. As teachers implement, they need planned opportunities where they discuss, refine, and compare their work and experiences. These follow-ups help build culture around instructional improvement by reinforcing the shared commitment to the hard work of improving instruction.

This approach to professional development will only work if teachers have the time to experiment, refine, and be honest about what’s going well and what’s not going well. Moreover, we can’t reasonably expect teachers to change everything at once. That’s a recipe for cognitive overload and failure, so leaders need to prioritize.

t: The Shaping of Expertise
q: The tapper is humming along in their head, hearing melody, harmony, even instrumentation. The listener hears only a dry tap-tap-tap. Expertise often feels like that: the expert believes they are transmitting a whole symphony, but the novice receives little more than noise.
Early education raises students' self-perceived expertise, and the frameworks they gain allow them to generate convincing interpretations of unfamiliar material, even when it is fictitious.
Novices lean heavily on their working memory: limited, fragile, easily overloaded. Experts, by contrast, draw upon rich, structured knowledge: “chunks” that compress complexity into manageable units.
For beginners, structure is a lifeline; for experts, it is a hindrance, creating redundancy and even cognitive overload. Educational psychologists call this the expertise reversal effect.

Deliberate practice is not mere repetition; it is a highly structured activity designed solely to improve performance. It requires intense, focused concentration on pushing beyond one's current limits, relies on constant feedback to identify and correct errors, and is inherently effortful rather than enjoyable.
Yes, it can contribute to distributed cognition: a system of people, tools, and symbols working together. But it does not carry responsibility, nor does it bear the consequences of its judgements.

t: Timothy Shanahan Points to a Possible Speech-to-Print Advantage
q: This union of phonemic awareness (PA) with phonics means our students are simultaneously focusing their attention on their language sounds and the letters and spellings representing those sounds. Discussing their 2024 meta-analysis, Florina Erbeli and Marianne Rice emphasize that both PA with and without letters improved phonemic awareness—but it was PA with letters that improved reading and spelling.

This distinction between auditory and visual signals may explain Timothy Shanahan’s stated disconnect between learning to read and reading, which seems counterintuitive until we consider that humans as a species began—and humans as individuals begin—speaking long before they began and begin reading. Therefore, reading instruction that recruits what the brain has been primed for might create the optimal conditions that promote efficient recognition of how letters represent speech.

Encoding is the entry point to learning how to decode. While we know that traditional phonics programs do include writing, in S2P writing is an integral part of reading to the extent that dictation often precedes practice with reading decodable text, and this approach teaches students to say the phonemes as they write the graphemes. Spelling is a noisy affair.

Speech-to-Print advocates like me have been satisfied for a long time despite lack of definitive proof because we see how much more efficient this approach is, even if it is only equally effective as the best P2S approaches.

Steve Dykstra cautions that a lack of bullseye evidence for a particular instructional method shouldn’t automatically rule out that method if it can be part of making reasonable decisions that we believe will benefit our students. He says: We are not required to be right; we are required to have ‘right’ reasons that we can explain to other professionals . . . Know where the science ends and your best judgment begins.

Finally—and most important—let’s cultivate curiosity and show humility as we examine the best reading instruction methods available. Let’s be highly selective and choose methods that align with best practices regardless of their origin, freeing decision-making from trends and traditions that may not be serving our students in the best possible ways.
There is too much tribalism and not enough trial and error in considering new and/or repurposed approaches to reading instruction. Let’s make changes that really make a difference. That’s the point.

t: Planning Instruction with the Willingham Simple Memory Model: A Lesson on World Regions
q: One of the central findings from cognitive science is that learning is inseparable from memory. If nothing has been retained in long-term memory, then no learning has occurred.

When I plan lessons, I now use the model as a kind of cognitive checklist. It forces me to ask: What will students actually attend to? How do I prevent working memory overload? How will I promote durable encoding, retrieval, and resistance to forgetting?
This structured environment reduces cognitive interference from unnecessary items and keeps attention directed towards instruction.
Cognitive science shows that explaining to others is a powerful form of rehearsal: it requires retrieval, comparison, and organization, all of which strengthen memory traces.

In addition, students create flashcards for the key terms (region, physical region, cultural region, economic region) with definitions and examples. These cards feed into the Leitner flashcard system, ensuring that their schema is not only built but also reinforced through spaced retrieval.

It reminds me that learning is not equivalent to exposure. Students do not learn because material was “covered” in class. They learn because information passed through working memory, was encoded into long-term memory, and was later retrieved and reinforced.

For me as a teacher, the model is both a warning and a guide. The warning is that without attention, encoding, and retrieval, content will be forgotten, regardless of how engaging my lesson feels. The guide is that if I deliberately design instruction to align with each stage of the model, I dramatically increase the likelihood that students will not just understand content temporarily but retain it, retrieve it, and use it to build further knowledge.

t: The Paradox of Memory: Why Forgetting Makes Learning Possible
q: In Borges' short story Funes the Memorious, the protagonist is cursed with a perfect memory: every leaf on a tree, every fleeting sensation, every trivial detail is preserved. But this gift renders him incapable of thought. With nothing forgotten, nothing can be abstracted, compared, or made meaningful.

A fact can feel inaccessible in the moment (low retrieval strength) but still be deeply encoded (high storage strength). Crucially, each successful act of effortful retrieval increases both. That is why the temporary forgetting we experience between practice sessions actually enhances learning.
In contrast, testing yourself on that same material, even if you fail at first, creates the conditions for storage strength to grow. Effort, not ease, is the signal of long-term learning.

The irony is that the methods that produce the most immediate fluency such as re-reading, highlighting, immediate review, often create the illusion of learning without building lasting retention. Students feel confident because information is readily accessible in working memory, but this accessibility is temporary. The moment the external cues disappear, so does the knowledge.

The Bjorks’ work reveals that forgetting isn't a failure of the memory system, it's an adaptive feature. Our brains are constantly making decisions about what deserves long-term storage. Information that gets repeatedly retrieved and used is marked as important and strengthened.

Perhaps most importantly, this adaptive forgetting creates the conditions for abstraction and generalisation. By allowing specific details to fade while preserving general patterns, our memory system enables us to extract principles, recognise similarities across different contexts, and apply knowledge flexibly.
Far from being the enemy of memory, forgetting then is what makes memory possible. If we remembered everything equally, nothing would stand out. Memory works by filtering, not stockpiling.

t: The Most Expensive Word When You’re Chasing an Impossible Goal
q: I kept saying yes to partnerships, projects, and collaborations, thinking more was better. It felt like I was building momentum. In reality, I was just building noise.

Instead of ruthlessly protecting my resources for the moves that would fix the root problem, I said yes to an ‘opportunity’ that looked like a quick fix. I bought into the ‘expert’ telling me what I needed to do, and I agreed and tried to go as fast as possible.

When you have a big, audacious, impossible goal, every yes costs something. And that cost is almost always time you can’t get back.

t: 5 Shifts I Made in my Phonemic Awareness Instruction
q: After administering the screener and looking at the results, I was taken aback with the PSF (Phoneme Segmentation Fluency) scores. Seventy-nine percent of my students were far below or below grade level.

If using manipulatives helped me understand how to break apart the sounds, I knew I needed to try this with my students immediately. I gave each of my students 5 colored tiles to keep in their desks so we could use them when needed.

After giving the middle of the year screener and seeing how 75% of students were able to segment the sounds without manipulatives, I started fading them away and mostly used them for certain students and/or in small groups. Students who were not using manipulatives would show me how many sounds on their fingers.

There is a time and place for practicing things like rhyming words, and counting syllables, but focusing on segmenting and blending every single day helped my class tremendously. Every day we would segment and blend at least 5-10 words.

When I was following Heggarty “with fidelity” it usually did not match what we were doing during the rest of our word study block. I decided to jazz things up by intentionally adding in 3-5 words to segment and blend that aligned with our current phonics instruction.

One easy way I did that during phonemic awareness was adding 2-3 words at least a few times a week with concepts we were going to be studying in the upcoming weeks. It was almost like building some background knowledge before introducing a new phonics concept.

t: “Well-Organised Misunderstanding": The Fine Art of Being Wrong
q: When I first started teaching almost 20 years ago, I used to think that when students gave wrong answers, they simply lacked the correct knowledge, that misconceptions were just gaps to be filled. But then I encountered Michelene Chi's work, and I realised I was wrong about being wrong.

In other words, you can't overwrite a misconception with a fact; you have to confront and replace the flawed model itself. Contradiction is key. For change to happen, students must recognise that what they believed is incompatible with the correct view.
This resonates deeply with my own experience of marking student work. I've seen students make surface-level corrections while maintaining the same fundamental errors across multiple attempts.

In other words, reasoning skill alone doesn’t guarantee accurate reasoning. As Daniel Willingham has pointed out, critical thinking is not a generic set of moves that float free of content. We think critically about something, and the quality of that thinking depends on the accuracy and depth of the knowledge we bring to bear.

If we want students to think critically, we must first make sure they are thinking with the right concepts. That means identifying, surfacing, and, when necessary, dismantling flawed mental models, not just teaching abstract heuristics about argument and evidence. Otherwise, we risk creating highly articulate students who can argue brilliantly… for things that aren’t true.

For example, the "I do, we do, you do" structure isn't just about gradual release of responsibility, it's about gradual revelation of student thinking. During the "we do" phase, teachers can observe student responses, catch misconceptions early, and provide immediate corrective feedback before errors become entrenched. This is conceptual change in real time.

Chi's framework reminds us that behind every persistent error lies a logical system trying to make sense of the world. So I guess our job isn't to dismiss that logic but to understand it well enough to help students build something better.

t: You Can’t System Your Way Out of the Wrong People
q: I’m going to say something I wish someone had forced me to hear sooner: It’s not just about the systems. It’s about who’s running them.

You can have the cleanest SOPs, the smartest tech stack, the most well-architected execution model, but if the people executing it aren’t aligned, accountable, or capable… it breaks. Or worse, it drains you while slowly killing the vision.
Over the years, I’ve held onto people way too long. And it wasn’t because they were the right fit. Usually it was because I liked them.
I’ve kept people who were good at something, just not the thing we actually needed. I’ve made excuses, told myself I was being too harsh, and lowered the bar more than once.

Hiring a B player doesn’t just hurt output; it breaks culture. Keeping someone misaligned teaches the rest of the team that your standards aren’t real. Your systems are only as strong as the people upholding them.
But loyalty without clarity becomes martyrdom. And you weren’t put on this planet to die on the hill of someone else’s unfulfilled potential.
The right people make the systems sing. The wrong people make the systems feel like more work.

t: Maximizing Instructional Time Through Routines and Rehearsal
q: Time is our most precious resource. Each day, our students grow older, and the calendar moves forward. When our 180 days are up, we will send them off to the next class, whether we maximized our time with them or let it slip through our fingers.

36 minutes can seem like a lot of time, but if you added up the time it takes to transition between subjects, to get from chair to carpet, to get out materials, to wait for the class to get quiet before speaking, to clean up and get ready for lunch/specials/recess, to pack up at the end of the day, etc. you’d be surprised how quickly 36 minutes can sneak up on you.

Additionally, when I’m actively teaching, the task of giving the instruction takes up so little of my working memory that I’m able to focus on my students and their needs throughout the lesson. Lastly, I find it very easy when I have student-teachers in the room to train them to take over my routines, since they are so clearly defined and laid out.

The high level of predictability gives them an instant dose of success, because even when content is new, they always know how to do our different tasks. I also believe this consistency provides a sense of psychological safety for my students.

The first time we rehearse a task, we repeat it however many times it takes until every child is able to complete it exactly as I’d like. Between each attempt, I provide corrective feedback to refine their understanding of the task, along with additional modeling of the task as needed.
If you allow a behavior once, be prepared to allow it a thousand times more. This consistency means beyond the first few weeks of school, I rarely have to call my students back to repeat a direction.

Getting these routines rehearsed perfectly from the start is crucial so that no instructional time is wasted moving forward. Whatever time you save cutting corners at the start will be more than lost by the end of the year due to disruptions that come after.

t: I Let My Team Fall Apart, On Purpose
q: But I’ve learned something over the years: If you’re always the safety net, your team will never learn to land on their feet.

Disagreements aren’t dysfunction. They’re often the signs of people caring deeply and trying to figure things out. If you intervene too early, you risk creating compliance instead of commitment.
It’s not about being absent. It’s about being strategically invisible: strong in presence, but subtle in control. Like a climbing rope: always there, only tightening when someone slips.
But great leadership isn’t about shielding people. It’s about believing in them enough to let them struggle, and letting that struggle become their teacher.

t: The Music of Learning: Resonance, Relationship, and the Emotions of Education
q: Resonance is the feeling of being moved by something and responding in a way that changes you. It’s an acoustic metaphor: one thing vibrates in response to another.

Rather than treating it as the transmission of knowledge or the acquisition of discrete skills, resonant education invites us to see learning as a deeply human, relational, emotional, and transformative process. It asks us to reimagine the classroom as a space where meaningful encounters can occur: between learners and ideas, between students and teachers, and between people and the world.

First comes engagement, when the learner is struck by something: a question, a story, a moment of dissonance. Then follows reflection, as the experience incubates and deepens. Illumination comes next, often as a flash of insight or a subtle shift in understanding.
Resonance and rigour are not mutually exclusive. What Rosa and Biesta both caution against is the reduction of education to performance, control, and outcomes.

Taken as a whole, research studies show that emotions are not just messy toddlers in a china shop, running around breaking and obscuring delicate cognitive glassware. Instead, emotions are more like the shelves underlying the glassware; without them cognition has less support.

Universities have long privileged ‘cold cognition’. But both the classroom and the world of practice are fundamentally places of ‘warm cognition’. It is impossible for humans to build memories, engage in complex thoughts, or make meaningful decisions without the involvement of emotions.

Equally important is the relationship between students and educators. Teaching is a human interaction, and emotions are central to how students experience that relationship. When students feel heard, supported, and respected, their emotional well-being improves, and so does their capacity to learn.

t: How Two Teachers Brought the Science of Learning to their District
q: In-house professional development is very much valued in our district, but the time to commit to it is often the barrier. Tara and I knew that this could be a successful workshop, but we didn’t want it to come across as a fad or a trend. We knew the science of learning was grounded in research, but we had to teach our participants this in a way where they could make connections to what they were already doing and activate prior knowledge.

Our 18 hour class was broken up into six 2 hour sessions, plus six hours of independent work to receive inservice credit or PDP’s. Our participants were 32 K-6 educators, ranging from Classroom Teachers, Special Educators, Speech and Language Pathologists, and Multilingual teachers. Our regional district has six elementary schools, and we had at least one participant from each of them.

This was our first go at sharing our passions about learning science and feeding others what we thought would enhance their teaching practices. This was where it got fun but also messy - we wanted to share the nuts and bolts about the science of learning but also knew that providing our participants with the knowledge to approach activities with the students in front of them was essential.

We wanted to have touchpoints so there could be a connection to previous knowledge. Therefore, the topics that we shared could be built on one another but also then applied to new approaches educators could use with their students.

Application by our participants was a key piece of our workshop. After each face-to-face session, they completed independent assignments ranging from reading articles, listening to podcasts, watching videos, composing poems, completing activities with their students, and a rose, bud, and thorn reflection.

I would get emails and texts from our participants raving about the podcasts. They also sent photos showcasing student work. Braindumps, hexagonal thinking activities connecting to content, and engaging activities and games to highlight retrieval practices - oh my!

We hope that the district will continue to build on what Tara and I started. Many colleagues have asked for a Part 2! We learned so much, and our colleagues started to bring it back to our students. Throughout this process, we kept saying “If only we knew this when we were first starting out in our careers…

t: Don't Predict My Politics Based on My Pedagogy

Doing my job means acknowledging assets and addressing deficits. I’m not making a political statement, I’m just giving my students what they need to succeed.

t: Why Struggle Still Matters in a Digital Age
q: Research suggests that many students believe learning should be fixed, simple, certain, and quick. When learning feels effortful, they may misinterpret that struggle as a sign of failure, not progress.

What’s remarkable is that even without conscious attention, errors can prompt the brain to adapt. Mistakes, in other words, are catalysts for neuroplasticity. They prime the brain to rewire, especially during sleep, helping us grow.

One way to harness the power of error is through “productive failure.” For example, instead of starting with instruction, this method can begin with problem-solving, even if students haven’t yet fully learned the concepts. Struggling upfront fosters deeper understanding later.

The same holds true for what cognitive scientists call “desirable difficulties.” Spacing out practice, switching between tasks, or self-testing while studying all make learning harder in the moment but better in the long run. These techniques pose a paradox: they feel like they’re not working. Performance dips in the short term. But when it’s time to apply knowledge, learners who embraced difficulty outperform those who played it safe.

A recent chapter by Barbara Oakley and colleagues pushes back against the idea that memorisation is obsolete in the digital age. Relying too heavily on “cognitive offloading” can undermine our ability to think fluently, spot errors, or apply knowledge creatively.

Generative AI gives the impression that knowledge is now instant. With the right prompt, we can summon answers, generate summaries, or solve complex problems. But this convenience creates an illusion: that mastery can be downloaded.

In the end, human learning is embodied, emotional, social, and deeply contextual. Our minds are shaped by our bodies, our histories, our relationships, and the environments we move through. Emotions like curiosity and belonging ignite learning. Culture and lived experience shape how we think, what we value, and how we grow.

t: The Visualizer and My Three Amigos: A Perfect Match
q: The result I hope to achieve? A classroom where students feel more confident engaging with complex content, and where expert-level thinking is no longer invisible, it’s shared, practiced, and ultimately, internalized.

Rosenshine emphasized the power of modeling, guided practice, and scaffolding. A visualizer allows me to do all three with clarity and precision. I can model expert strategies in real time, walk students through guided steps with shared visuals, and scaffold new concepts by chunking information in a way that matches their current level of understanding.

Sweller and Cognitive Load Theory reminds us that learning happens best when we manage the mental effort students must exert. The visualizer helps me reduce extraneous load by making instructions and explanations clearer and more concrete. It also helps me support intrinsic load by unpacking complex material into smaller, manageable parts, and showing students not only what to learn, but how to think.

Ausubel, whose theory of meaningful learning is at the heart of my model, argued that new knowledge is most effectively learned when it can be anchored to prior knowledge. The visualizer helps me do just that. It makes abstract ideas visible and allows me to build clear, explicit connections between what students already know and what they are learning next.
